# Chapter 1: The Wound in the Wall

*Satoshi*

The wound in the wall had been there for as long as anyone in the village could remember, and nobody agreed on what had caused it.

A crack ran from the base of the ridge down through the granite face, wide enough at the top to fit a man's shoulders and narrowing to a finger's width where it met the riverbed.
Water came through it in spring, clear and cold, and in winter it froze into a curtain of ice that caught the low sun and held it long enough to make the whole village look like it was being watched through glass.

I stood at the inn's upper window and looked at it the way I had looked at it every morning for the better part of a year now.
The scar along my jaw pulled tight, a small hot flare I felt a half-breath before I understood why.
Nobody else in the room noticed anything change.

Dieter went on with his ale, and old Kenzo kept watching the road, same as every day.
Chiyo was somewhere in the back arguing gently with a delivery boy about the weight of a sack of flour.

Then the air coming through the gap in the shutter turned, for perhaps three seconds, into something with a mineral edge to it, cold and faintly metallic, like a coin held too long in a closed fist.
Underneath that was a second smell I did not have a clean word for: sweet, the kind spoiled things are before they are anything else.

It was gone before I had set the tray down.
The ordinary woodsmoke and yeast smell of the common room closed back over both like water over a dropped stone.

---

"Someone's posted a notice at the district board," Kenzo said.

He had not moved from the window in some hours, which was not unusual.
What was unusual was that he sat frowning at something on the road that was not, as far as I could tell, actually there yet.

"Dieter's clerk friend was up putting fresh paper over the old one an hour past.
Official seal on it, the round one, not the town seal."

"People post things," I said, and took his cup before he could ask twice for more ale he had already had enough of.

"Not usually with two soldiers standing over the man while he does it."
He turned from the window at last, and there was something in his face I did not often see there, an old man's flat, unhopeful attention, the look he otherwise reserved for weather that meant to be bad.
"They're sending someone into the valley, girl.
That's the shape of it.
First time since it happened.
I'd wager the whole grain allowance on it."

By then the light outside had gone the flat pewter it turned every evening this time of year, the kind that made the whole village look like it was remembering something rather than living it.
Chiyo had banked the fire and sent the cart drivers off to their delayed cargo and was counting the day's coin at the counter with the particular satisfaction of a woman who liked her totals to come out even.

"Into the mist?" she said, without pausing her counting.
"What in the Kami's name would anyone want in there."

"What anyone from the Empire ever wants," Kenzo said, and did not finish the thought, which was its own kind of answer.

*I want back in.*

I let myself think it in exactly those plain words, once, then glanced at Chiyo before I buried it again with the rest of what I did not examine too closely.
I felt her eyes on the back of my head, and did not turn.

"Well," I said, and put the cup away.
"I suppose we'll know soon enough."

---

The road out of Kiriguchi climbed north for two kilometers before it bent east toward the ridge, and I walked it the way I walked most things now: quickly, without looking back, with one hand resting on the line of the scar without my having decided to put it there.

The mist wall was visible from the bend in the road, a pale line standing at the head of the valley where the land folded upward and the road gave out.
From this distance it looked almost gentle, a bank of morning fog that had simply forgotten to burn off by noon.

I had stopped telling people what it actually was.
They found out soon enough on their own, usually from someone who had lost a father or a flock to it, and by then nothing I said improved the lesson.

The scar flared again, hot and quick, and this time I did not wait for it to pass.
I turned toward the mist and stood still.

It was waiting.
Not the way a predator waits, not the way weather waits.
The way a question waits for someone to stop avoiding the answer.

*I know you*, I thought, and the thought arrived with a certainty that had no source, the same sourceless knowing that had put the scar on my face and the word *Okiri* in my mouth the first time I had woken in this valley with no memory of how I got here.

The mist moved.
Not toward me. Not away.
It shifted, the way a curtain shifts when someone behind it turns their head, and for one held breath I saw a shape in it that was not mist, a figure standing just inside the wall with its back to me, perfectly still.

Then it was gone, and the road was empty, and the wind came off the ridge carrying nothing but the smell of wet stone and the faint mineral edge of something I could not name.

I stood there for a long time after that.
The light changed.
The mist did not.
